name: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (ATXN7, with retinopathy)
aliases: autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia with retinal degeneration

clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant ataxia distinguished from all other SCAs by a progressive cone-rod retinal dystrophy causing central visual loss and eventual blindness
Caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN7 producing an expanded polyglutamine ataxin-7 protein
Shows striking anticipation; large expansions can present with a severe infantile form featuring failure to thrive and rapid multisystem decline
Visual symptoms (impaired colour vision, reduced acuity, central scotoma) may precede, coincide with, or follow the onset of ataxia
Fundoscopy shows macular changes and pigmentary maculopathy; the electroretinogram reveals cone-then-rod dysfunction
Cerebellar ataxia is accompanied by dysarthria, dysphagia, pyramidal signs and slowed saccades
The combination of cerebellar ataxia with retinal degeneration should prompt directed ATXN7 testing
Care is multidisciplinary and supportive, including low-vision rehabilitation, physiotherapy and swallowing assessment
reference.pathophysiology: SCA7 is caused by expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in ATXN7, translated into an elongated polyglutamine tract in the ataxin-7 protein, a component of transcriptional coactivator complexes. The mutant protein misfolds, forms nuclear inclusions and disrupts transcriptional regulation, producing toxic gain-of-function degeneration. Unlike other polyglutamine SCAs, ataxin-7 dysfunction also injures retinal photoreceptors, giving the characteristic cone-rod dystrophy alongside degeneration of the cerebellum, brainstem and spinal tracts. The repeat is highly unstable, especially on paternal transmission, underlying pronounced anticipation and severe early-onset cases.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxias without retinopathy (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3)
Retinitis pigmentosa or isolated cone-rod dystrophy from other causes
Mitochondrial disorders combining ataxia and retinal degeneration
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis and other neurodegenerations with visual loss
Abetalipoproteinaemia and vitamin E deficiency ataxia with retinopathy
Paraneoplastic syndromes affecting cerebellum and retina
additionalInvestigations: Formal ophthalmological assessment with fundoscopy, colour vision testing and visual fields
Electroretinography and optical coherence tomography to characterise the retinal dystrophy
MRI brain showing cerebellar and brainstem (olivopontocerebellar) atrophy
Nerve conduction studies to assess associated tract involvement
Metabolic and vitamin screening to exclude treatable mimics
redFlags: Infantile or early-childhood presentation with failure to thrive and rapid deterioration indicating a large expansion
Rapidly progressive visual loss threatening independence and safety
Marked anticipation across a pedigree signalling risk of a severe phenotype in offspring
reference.prognosis: Prognosis correlates with repeat size: adult-onset disease progresses over one to a few decades with combined visual and motor disability, whereas large expansions cause severe infantile disease with early death. Blindness and loss of ambulation are common in advanced cases.
pitfalls: Investigating cerebellar ataxia and visual loss as separate problems and missing the unifying diagnosis
Omitting an eye examination in a patient with dominant ataxia, thereby overlooking the key discriminating feature
Underestimating anticipation when counselling families about offspring risk
Mistaking the retinal dystrophy for simple age-related macular degeneration
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive across the neurological and visual domains
Physiotherapy with gait and balance rehabilitation, and occupational therapy for mobility aids and falls
Speech and language therapy for dysarthria, with proactive management of dysphagia including nutritional support and aspiration prevention
Ophthalmology-led low-vision rehabilitation and visual aids for the progressive cone-rod dystrophy, with support towards eventual blindness
Regular ophthalmological and neurological surveillance to track retinal and motor progression, monitoring for aspiration and weight loss
In the severe infantile form, paediatric multidisciplinary care addressing feeding, failure to thrive and rapid multisystem decline
Genetic counselling emphasising anticipation, particularly on paternal transmission, with cascade and predictive testing
